Well, my experience was pretty simple. My wife's father didn't expect me to ask permission I guess -- he didn't have much of a father from what I recall, so I guess it was just sort of lost on him. I called him up one day when i was at college (trips home weren't really possible financially at the time, otherwise i would have done it in person) and asked him over the phone. He was surprised -- not because he thought i was rude or discourteous, but because he just didn't expect to be asked. I just told him that I knew how much [my wife] valued him and his opinion and that I did too and wanted to make sure it was ok with him before i asked her. Her father and I are on very good terms.

Good on you for doing it, don't listen to all the idiots who are trying to make it into a big deal like you're treating her as property. I had to do this, because my father in law is actually from "the old world". Here are my thoughts:

-- I didn't just "have to" do it, I wanted to. I was proud to. There are just some moments in life where standing up like a man gives a very satisfying feeling of honor and dignity. -- If you are serious about getting married you should already have prepared yourself by being financially stable, not just employed, but on a career path, and ready for the lifestyle change that comes with being married. --If you have prepared yourself accordingly (as mentioned above), you should be able to stand before him and say with confidence who and what you are, what you want, and what your plans are. As a father of a daughetr, I can tell you for sure that no father wants to hand his little girl over to someone who isn't prepared, hasn't thought the whole thing through in a real sense, or doesn't have balls enough to stand up and be a man and present himself to me. -- Altough many will disagree, you are not just asking for a blessing. If you are truly being honorable you are asking for permission. A father that sees you are prepared, of good character, and dedicated to his daughter will give his permission. Some fathers might not give it so easily but may test you first. Earn their permission as an act of good faith. They will respect you for it. The daughter, your future wife will also respect you for it and love you even more for trying so hard to be in good standing with her family. -- Also very important and many overlook, if accepted, you should make an honest attempt at fitting in with the elder males of her family, grandfathers, uncles etc. They are the ones who will be your biggest allies if things get hard at times. They will also be the guys you hang out with watching sports and such during family gatherings.

Good luck, and I wish the best for the two of you.

Be very candid and respectful. Hopefully you don't dress like a douche or act obnoxious.

He wants to see that you are ready for the responsibility of being married. When my kids bring home someone for me to meet, I'll expect they act mature, are stable, can hold a conversation, etc.

You're expecting this guy to hand over a beautiful product of his family. You are asking to become a part of the family. Show him that you can fit into the family without anyone regretting it.

Be a respectable adult, Cook on the barbecue, make pancakes for breakfast, be the man that you would respect, help with chores, show interest in other peoples hobbies or interests.

I believe this is a contemporary ritual of respect, left over from an expected requirement from days when a father/husband had the final say in all things family related. In turn, such signs of respect can be expressed by future father-in-laws. Long before asking, my father-in-law presented me a really nice pocket knife. This an old tradition of male bonding / acceptance between men. I'd not been aware of it and was quite humbled by it. All in all, signs of mutual respect are the desired result.
